lessons.title: Wi-Fi and 802.11
lessons.summary: How Wi-Fi shares the air with CSMA/CA, why hidden terminals need RTS/CTS, how channels interfere, what Wi-Fi 4 to 7 changed, and why advertised aggregate PHY rates differ from application throughput.
lessons.body:
Switched Ethernet commonly gives each device a dedicated wired link. Wi-Fi stations share radio resources, but not every station can hear every other. Modern multi-user techniques allow coordinated simultaneous transmissions, and spatial reuse can allow concurrent transmissions in different coverage areas. Radio conditions change with interference, motion and obstacles.

Almost everything distinctive about Wi-Fi follows from that: how devices take turns, why they cannot detect collisions, how a slow active client can consume airtime needed by another client, and why a product’s aggregate advertised PHY rates do not predict one client’s application throughput.

## The 802.11 generations

Wi-Fi is the Wi-Fi Alliance's brand for the IEEE **802.11** standards. In 2018 the Alliance introduced generation numbers so people did not need to remember letters.

| Name | Standard | Bands | Key additions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Legacy | 802.11b/a/g | b/g: 2.4; a: 5 GHz | b up to 11 Mbit/s; a/g up to 54, with OFDM for a/g |
| Wi-Fi 4 | 802.11n (2009) | 2.4, 5 GHz | MIMO, 40 MHz, aggregation |
| Wi-Fi 5 | 802.11ac (2013) | 5 GHz | 80/160 MHz, 256-QAM, DL MU-MIMO |
| Wi-Fi 6 | 802.11ax; certification began 2019 | 2.4, 5 GHz | OFDMA, 1024-QAM, TWT |
| Wi-Fi 6E | 802.11ax | adds 6 GHz | additional spectrum, subject to local rules |
| Wi-Fi 7 | 802.11be; certification began 2024 | 2.4, 5, 6 GHz | 320 MHz, 4096-QAM, MLO |

What each change buys:

- **MIMO** (multiple-input multiple-output): several antennas send independent **spatial streams** on the same frequency at once. Two streams roughly double the rate. The usable count depends on both endpoints and the radio channel; antenna count alone does not establish it.
- **Wider channels**: rate scales roughly with width, so 80 MHz carries about four times a 20 MHz channel.
- **Denser modulation (QAM)**: 256-QAM carries 8 bits per symbol, 1024-QAM 10, 4096-QAM 12. Each step needs a much cleaner signal, so achievable modulation depends on signal quality, interference and hardware, not a fixed distance boundary.
- **OFDMA** (Wi-Fi 6): the channel is split into **resource units**, so the AP can send to or receive from several clients in one transmission instead of one at a time. This can reduce per-client access overhead, depending on scheduling, compatible clients and workload.
- **Target Wake Time** (Wi-Fi 6): devices negotiate when to wake, saving battery for phones and IoT sensors.
- **6 GHz** (Wi-Fi 6E and 7): additional spectrum for capable devices, subject to national power, indoor/outdoor and coexistence rules. It is not interference-free. Country allocations change: for example, Ofcom published a July 2026 upper-6-GHz sharing decision, so an undated “UK has only 500 MHz” statement is inadequate.
- **Multi-Link Operation** (Wi-Fi 7): coordinates multiple links; concurrent transmission/reception depends on the MLO mode and hardware. It does not require every device to transmit on three bands simultaneously.

## Sharing the air: CSMA/CA

Classic shared Ethernet used **CSMA/CD**: listen before sending, and if you *detect a collision* while transmitting, stop, jam and back off. Wi-Fi cannot do the "CD" part:

1. Ordinary Wi-Fi radios do not implement Ethernet-style collision detection while sending; their own transmit signal makes simultaneous sensing of weak incoming signals difficult.
2. A collision may happen at the receiver but not be audible at the sender at all (see hidden terminals below).

So Wi-Fi tries to **avoid** collisions instead, and uses missing expected acknowledgments as an indication of failure; not every frame is individually acknowledged. The following is a simplified **DCF** contention example for acknowledged unicast using 5 GHz OFDM timings. Modern QoS traffic commonly uses EDCA with access-category parameters; broadcast/multicast and scheduled multi-user exchanges differ:

1. **Carrier sense.** Listen. If the channel is busy, wait until it goes idle.
2. **Wait DIFS.** After the channel goes idle, wait a fixed gap (34 µs on 5 GHz).
3. **Random backoff.** Pick a random number of slots in `[0, CW]` (9 µs slots; CW starts at 15). Count down only while the channel stays idle; freeze the counter if someone else starts sending.
4. **Transmit** when the counter hits zero.
5. **ACK.** The receiver replies after a shorter gap, SIFS (16 µs). The shorter gap gives priority over compliant contenders that sense this exchange; interference and hidden terminals can still corrupt the ACK.
6. **No ACK?** Assume a collision or corruption, grow CW as `min(2 × (CW + 1) − 1, CWmax)` (here 15, 31, 63 ... up to 1023) and try again. After a retry limit, drop the frame.

```
busy |DIFS| backoff |  DATA  |SIFS|ACK|
-----+----+---------+--------+----+---+
      34us  k x 9us           16us
```

There is also **virtual carrier sense**: eligible frames carry Duration/ID information that can reserve remaining exchange time. Stations update their **NAV** (network allocation vector) according to protocol rules. Some fields are zero or have other meanings; physical carrier sensing still applies.

> [!note] Why the random backoff matters
> If two stations both wait for a busy channel to end and then send immediately, they can collide when their transmissions overlap at the receiver. The random countdown spreads them out, and the doubling makes stations back off harder when the channel is congested.

## The hidden terminal problem and RTS/CTS

Carrier sense only works if every station can hear every other. Often they cannot.

```
  (A) ~~~~~~ [AP] ~~~~~~ (C)
   A hears AP, C hears AP,
   A and C cannot hear each other
```

A and C both sense an idle channel and transmit at once. Their frames can interfere **at the AP**, causing missing ACKs and retries. Capture effects or different timings can allow some frames to succeed; throughput need not collapse in every such topology.

**RTS/CTS** can mitigate this when the relevant contenders receive the protection frames:

1. A sends a short **Request To Send** to the AP, with the duration of the exchange.
2. The AP replies **Clear To Send**, also carrying the duration.
3. C cannot hear A's RTS, but it *can* hear the AP's CTS, so it sets its NAV and stays quiet.
4. A sends its data; the AP ACKs.

This reduces the chance of wasting a long data transmission on a hidden-terminal collision. Missed CTS frames, other interferers and overlapping reservations still permit data/ACK loss. The cost is two extra frames and gaps per exchange, so implementations can select protection using an **RTS threshold** and other policies; defaults are device-specific. Wi-Fi 6 also uses RTS/CTS-style protection automatically in some situations, such as before multi-user transmissions.

The mirror image is the **exposed terminal**: a station that hears a nearby transmission and defers, even though its own transmission would not have interfered at its intended receiver. RTS/CTS does not fix this; it is one reason dense networks waste airtime.

## Channels and interference

**2.4 GHz** has channels only 5 MHz apart, but each transmission is about 20 MHz wide. Neighbouring channels therefore overlap, and **1, 6 and 11** is a conventional conservative 20 MHz plan where those channels are permitted. Available channels, PHY spectral masks and interference determine other viable plans; this is not the only possible set worldwide.

```
ch  1     6     11
  [====][====][====]
     [====]
    ch 3 overlaps both 1 and 6
```

Two kinds of interference behave very differently:

- **Co-channel**: your neighbour's AP is also on channel 6. When networks can sense each other, contention helps them share airtime. Collisions, hidden terminals and decoding failures can still occur.
- **Adjacent-channel**: your neighbour is on channel 3. Overlapping energy may interfere without successful frame decoding. Energy detection can still cause deferral, depending on thresholds. The result depends on power, frequency separation, placement and equipment; it is not a universal ranking of channel plans.

> [!tip] Rule of thumb
> In a dense deployment using channels 1–11, 20 MHz with a coordinated 1/6/11 plan is a useful starting point. Check the regulatory domain and survey neighbouring use; wider channels reduce the number of separate channels available.

**5 GHz** has many more 20 MHz channels, enough for several 80 MHz channels. Some are **DFS** channels shared with radar: an AP must listen for radar before using them and vacate if it detects any, which can cause a sudden channel change.

**6 GHz** excludes older 2.4/5-GHz-only Wi-Fi clients, but compatible clients can still use low rates or consume substantial airtime. Other authorised services and neighbouring networks may share spectrum.

At fixed antenna gains and distance, free-space path loss grows with frequency. Actual coverage also depends on permitted power, antenna patterns, wall materials, bandwidth and receiver sensitivity; a frequency label alone does not establish range or throughput. Other things share 2.4 GHz too: Bluetooth, microwave ovens and baby monitors.

## Why real throughput is far below the advertised rate

The number on the box is the **maximum PHY rate**, often summed across bands. Take an "AX3000" router:

- 5 GHz: 2 streams × 160 MHz × 1024-QAM ≈ 2,402 Mbit/s
- 2.4 GHz: 2 streams × 40 MHz ≈ 574 Mbit/s
- Total on the box: ~3,000. A conventional single-link client connection does not obtain this sum. Multiple-radio devices and other aggregation arrangements existed before Wi-Fi 7; MLO standardises coordinated multi-link operation.

Now follow the losses for a real phone.

### 1. The client's link rate is lower

For an example client with two spatial streams using an 80 MHz HE channel and 0.8 µs guard interval, full-channel single-stream PHY rates are approximately:

| MCS | Modulation | 1 stream, 80 MHz |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | BPSK 1/2 | 36 Mbit/s |
| 7 | 64-QAM 5/6 | 360 Mbit/s |
| 9 | 256-QAM 5/6 | 480 Mbit/s |
| 11 | 1024-QAM 5/6 | 600 Mbit/s |

Two rooms away, the phone might negotiate MCS 7 on 2 streams: about **720 Mbit/s**. **Rate adaptation** selects rates using link feedback; the illustrated room count does not predict a particular MCS.

### 2. MAC overhead

Every transmission pays a fixed cost in airtime: DIFS, average backoff, the PHY preamble, SIFS and the acknowledgement. For the calculation below, assume 200 µs per channel access and omit per-MPDU delimiters, padding and variable protocol costs. This is a supplied teaching value, not a universal measured overhead.

```
1 frame of 1500 B at 720 Mbit/s:
  data      12000 / 720e6 ~=   17 us
  overhead                ~=  200 us
  efficiency  17 / 217    ~=   8%

64 frames aggregated (A-MPDU):
  data      64 x 16.667   ~= 1067 us
  efficiency 1067 / 1267  ~=  84%
```

**Frame aggregation** amortises access costs; Block Ack can acknowledge multiple MPDUs. It is an important efficiency mechanism, but no single TCP/PHY efficiency percentage holds for every link.

### 3. Half duplex and sharing

An ordinary single radio link cannot simultaneously transmit and receive on that link. Uploads and downloads consume radio resources; scheduling, OFDMA/MU-MIMO, spatial reuse and multiple links make modern sharing more complex than a single global turn-taking sequence.

### 4. The performance anomaly

In a simplified saturated, equal-priority DCF model with comparable frame sizes, stations obtain similar access opportunities rather than equal airtime. Slow transmissions can then reduce faster stations’ throughput. QoS, aggregation, AP scheduling and airtime policies change this model.

> [!example] One slow client
> A fast client at 54 Mbit/s and a slow one at 6 Mbit/s alternate 1,500-byte frames. Ignoring overhead, a fast frame takes 222 µs and a slow one 2,000 µs. Each cycle of 2,222 µs moves one frame for each, so **both** get about 12,000 / 2,222 µs ≈ 5.4 Mbit/s. The fast client loses 90% of its throughput.

Some APs implement **airtime fairness** policies to mitigate this; capabilities and effectiveness vary. Moving compatible clients to another band can separate contention, but does not guarantee high rates there.

### 5. Loss and retries

Interference and fading cause corrupted frames. Wi-Fi retries at the link layer, which hides most loss from TCP but adds latency and jitter. Under load, large buffers in the AP add more: an illustrative loaded link might show 5 ms idle RTT and 200 ms during a download; this is not a universal measurement or unique diagnosis.

## Practical consequences
- Survey placement, interference, client capabilities and backhaul before changing settings. Wired backhaul avoids consuming wireless backhaul airtime; a dedicated radio still has coexistence and capacity constraints.
- Compare permitted bands for the actual devices and coverage needs. Extra APs need channel and power planning; more is not automatically better.
- Wired connections can remove active traffic from radio contention. An idle device’s removal need not produce a measurable improvement.
- Compare local wired and wireless tests, RSSI/SNR, negotiated rates, retries, airtime use and loaded latency to locate the bottleneck.

## Key takeaways
- Wi-Fi uses shared radio resources; modern multi-user and spatial-reuse mechanisms qualify simple one-transmitter models.
- Contention and acknowledgments reduce or reveal failures; they do not eliminate collisions.
- RTS/CTS can mitigate hidden terminals when protection is received and obeyed.
- A 1/6/11 plan is a common 2.4 GHz starting point, not a worldwide exclusivity rule.
- PHY rate, aggregate product labels and application throughput are different quantities. Rate, aggregation, scheduling, retries and backhaul all matter.

> [!note] Evidence limits
> Universal handset stream counts, fixed TCP efficiency ratios, driver defaults and guaranteed channel-plan outcomes are omitted because they need device-specific evidence. Regional spectrum rules are time-sensitive; consult the regulator before deployment. No RF, coverage, interference or throughput measurements were performed for this lesson.

questions.prompt: Why does ordinary Wi-Fi contention use collision avoidance rather than Ethernet-style detection of collisions during a transmission?

options.text: Wi-Fi frames are encrypted, so a radio cannot tell its own frame from a collision
options.explanation: Encryption protects the payload; it has nothing to do with sensing energy on the channel. Collision detection is a physical-layer problem, not a security one.

options.text: Its own transmission is vastly stronger at its antenna than any distant signal, so it cannot hear a collision while sending, and the collision may only happen at the receiver anyway
options.explanation: Correct. A transmitting radio is effectively deafened by itself, and with hidden terminals the collision happens at the receiver where the sender could never hear it. So Wi-Fi avoids collisions and infers failure from a missing ACK.

options.text: Radio waves travel too slowly for collisions to be detected in time
options.explanation: Radio travels at nearly the speed of light, faster than signals in copper. Propagation speed is not the obstacle.

options.text: 802.11 uses full-duplex radios, so collisions never happen
options.explanation: Wi-Fi is half duplex: a station sends or receives on a channel, not both. Collisions certainly happen, which is why exponential backoff exists.

questions.workedExample: The transmitting radio’s own signal makes sensing weak concurrent incoming signals difficult. More fundamentally, interference depends on what arrives at the receiver: hidden senders may not hear one another. Ordinary Wi-Fi uses carrier sensing, contention and missing expected ACKs instead of Ethernet-style collision detection. No fixed power ratio or claim about every possible radio design is needed.

questions.prompt: For three nearby 2.4 GHz APs restricted to channels 1–11 at 20 MHz width, which listed conventional channel plan avoids adjacent-channel overlap?

options.text: 1, 2 and 3
options.explanation: Adjacent 2.4 GHz channels are only 5 MHz apart, but each transmission is about 20 MHz wide, so 1, 2 and 3 overlap almost completely.

options.text: 1, 4 and 8
options.explanation: The 1-to-4 centre spacing is only 15 MHz. The conventional 1/6/11 plan provides 25 MHz between centres; exact interference also depends on spectral masks and equipment.
Correct among these choices. Centres at 2412, 2437 and 2462 MHz are 25 MHz apart. This is not a claim that no other valid plan exists worldwide.

options.text: Any three channels, because CSMA/CA stops them interfering
options.explanation: Carrier sensing cannot guarantee freedom from interference. Energy detection can defer even without decoding a frame, but overlapping channels still complicate coexistence.

questions.workedExample: Channels 1, 6 and 11 have centres 2412, 2437 and 2462 MHz, respectively: 25 MHz separation. That makes them the conventional non-overlapping selection among the offered plans for the stated domain. Other countries, PHYs and power arrangements require their own channel planning.

questions.prompt: A laptop (A) on one side of a warehouse and a scanner (C) on the other can both reach the AP in the middle, but not each other. Throughput collapses whenever both are busy. What is the standard 802.11 mechanism designed for this?

options.text: Increasing the DIFS gap on both stations
options.explanation: A longer common interframe wait does not reveal hidden transmissions or reserve the receiver; it does not directly solve the stated hidden-terminal problem.

options.text: RTS/CTS: the AP's Clear To Send is heard by both, so the other station sets its NAV and stays quiet
options.explanation: Correct. This is the hidden terminal problem. A and C cannot hear each other's RTS, but both hear the AP's CTS, which carries the duration of the exchange.

options.text: Switching both stations to CSMA/CD
options.explanation: Radios cannot detect collisions while transmitting, and in any case the collision happens at the AP, where neither sender can hear it.

options.text: Using a 40 MHz channel so there is room for both
options.explanation: Increasing channel width alone does not solve hidden-terminal contention. Coordinated multi-user mechanisms are separate from simply selecting a wider channel.

questions.workedExample: A and C can interfere at the AP without sensing one another. If C successfully receives and obeys the AP’s CTS, it defers for the protected interval while A sends. RTS/CTS can reduce wasted long-frame transmissions; missing protection frames, other interference and overlapping exchanges can still cause loss.

questions.prompt: Use the specified DCF model: CW starts at 15, grows as min(2(CW+1)−1, 1023) after each failed acknowledged transmission, and the retry limit permits another attempt. After three failures, what range supplies attempt four’s backoff?

options.explanation: That is the window for the first attempt only. Every missing ACK doubles the window, roughly.
That is the window for the third attempt (after two failures). Count the failures carefully: there have been three.
Correct. 15 → 31 after the first failure, 31 → 63 after the second, 63 → 127 after the third. The fourth attempt draws from [0, 127].
1023 is the cap the window can grow to, not where it jumps after a few failures.

questions.workedExample:
The window grows as CW = 2 × (CW + 1) − 1, i.e. 2^k − 1:

```
attempt 1: CW = 15     -> fail
attempt 2: CW = 31     -> fail
attempt 3: CW = 63     -> fail
attempt 4: CW = 127
```

So the station picks a random number of slots from 0 to 127. With 9 µs slots, that is up to 1.143 ms of countdown time. Busy-channel freezes and interframe waits can make elapsed time longer. The window grows for this contending station; not every other station necessarily changes its window.

questions.prompt: Two clients share one AP and alternate 1,500-byte frames. Client F's link rate is 300 Mbit/s; client S, at the edge of coverage, is at 30 Mbit/s. Ignoring MAC overhead, roughly what throughput does **F** get?

options.text: About 270 Mbit/s, because S only uses 10% of the capacity
options.explanation: The question explicitly supplies alternating equal-sized frames, not equal airtime. The slow frame occupies ten times as much transmission time.

options.text: About 150 Mbit/s, half the link rate
options.explanation: Halving would be right if both clients had the same link rate. S's slow frames take much more airtime than F's.

options.text: About 27 Mbit/s
options.explanation: Correct. Each cycle is one fast frame (40 µs) plus one slow frame (400 µs). 12,000 bits per 440 µs is about 27 Mbit/s for each client.

options.text: About 300 Mbit/s, since F's rate does not depend on S
options.explanation: F and S share one channel and take turns; time S spends on air is time F cannot use.

questions.workedExample:
1. Frame size: 1,500 B × 8 = 12,000 bits.
2. Airtime per frame:
   - F: 12,000 / 300 Mbit/s = 40 µs
   - S: 12,000 / 30 Mbit/s = 400 µs
3. They alternate, so one cycle = 40 + 400 = 440 µs and moves one frame for each.
4. Each client's throughput = 12,000 bits / 440 µs ≈ 27.3 Mbit/s.
5. F has lost over 90% of its potential. This illustrates the **performance anomaly** under the supplied model; suitable airtime scheduling can mitigate it, depending on implementation and traffic direction.

questions.prompt: In a controlled 2.4 GHz test, two APs on channel 1 decode one another and share airtime. Moving the neighbour to overlapping channel 2 or 3 instead causes substantial retries without useful coordination. Given these observed conditions and choices, which channel should the neighbour use?

options.text: Channel 3
options.explanation: The question supplies measured retry interference for channel 3; it is worse in this test. That is not a universal result for all powers and equipment.

options.text: Channel 1
options.explanation: Correct under the supplied observations: channel 1 permits useful coordination. Co-channel use still consumes airtime and does not eliminate collisions.

options.text: Channel 2
options.explanation: Channel 2 performed worse in the stated test. Energy detection and decoding behaviour vary by conditions.

options.text: All are equally harmful because the signal strength is the same
options.explanation: The scenario explicitly gives different measured outcomes. Equal received power alone does not determine interference or throughput.

questions.workedExample: Choose channel 1 from the supplied observations. Same-channel sensing can support coordinated deferral, while overlapping signals can cause interference. A proper survey should also test permissible non-overlapping options; neither co-channel safety nor adjacent-channel harm is absolute.

questions.prompt: An example AX3000 product label sums approximately 2,402 and 574 Mbit/s from two radios. A single-link, two-stream Wi-Fi 6 client achieves much less application throughput. Which factors can contribute? Select all that apply.

options.text: The label adds different radios’ maximum PHY rates, while this connection uses one link
options.explanation: Correct. The product aggregate is not the single-link application rate; multi-radio arrangements should not be ruled out merely by generation.

options.text: The phone negotiates a lower MCS (and perhaps 80 MHz rather than 160 MHz) because of distance and walls
options.explanation: Correct. For example, MCS 7 with two streams, 80 MHz and 0.8 µs GI gives roughly 720.6 Mbit/s PHY rate; obstacles alone do not determine this value.

options.text: Per-transmission MAC overhead, half duplex (TCP ACKs share the air) and other stations' airtime
options.explanation: Correct. Protocol overhead, radio-resource sharing and retransmissions affect goodput. There is no universal 50–70% ratio.

options.text: Wi-Fi spends time sending jam signals after every detected collision
options.explanation: Jam signals are CSMA/CD, from wired Ethernet. Wi-Fi cannot detect collisions and never sends jam signals.

options.text: TCP cannot use a window larger than 64 KB, which caps throughput at about 400 Mbit/s
options.explanation: TCP window scaling allows windows far beyond 64 KB, and in any case a 64 KB cap at a few ms RTT would give a different figure. It is not the reason.

questions.workedExample: A conditional example is: aggregate label near 3,000; one radio near 2,402; 80 MHz instead of 160 MHz near 1,201; MCS 7 at two streams/0.8 µs GI near 720.6 Mbit/s. Protocol overhead and other limits can reduce goodput further, but a fixed 0.6 multiplier is not a measured rule. Ethernet jam signals and a universal 64 KB TCP limit do not explain the gap.

questions.prompt: Assume each channel access costs about 200 µs of fixed overhead (DIFS, backoff, preamble, SIFS, Block Ack), and one 1,500-byte frame takes 17 µs of data airtime at your link rate. With A-MPDU aggregation of **32** frames per access, roughly what fraction of airtime carries data?

options.text: About 8%
options.explanation: That is the efficiency for a single unaggregated frame (17 / 217). Aggregation spreads the fixed cost across many frames.

options.text: About 73%
options.explanation: Correct. 32 × 17 = 544 µs of data per 744 µs access: 544 / 744 ≈ 73%.

options.text: About 97%
options.explanation: That would need the overhead to be tiny compared with the data. 200 µs against 544 µs of data is still a large chunk.

options.text: About 50%
options.explanation: 50% would mean data and overhead are equal, around 12 frames per access, not 32.

questions.workedExample:
1. Data airtime per access: 32 × 17 µs = 544 µs.
2. Total airtime per access: 544 + 200 = 744 µs.
3. Efficiency: 544 / 744 ≈ 0.73.

Compare:

```
frames  data   total  eff
  1      17     217    8%
 32     544     744   73%
 64    1088    1288   84%
```

This supplied model illustrates aggregation’s benefit. Real overhead also includes per-MPDU fields, padding, acknowledgments and scheduling details; both PHY rate and aggregation matter.

questions.prompt: In a simplified same-channel topology, B sends to A while C wants to send to D. Assume concurrent data transmissions would not interfere at either receiver. C nevertheless senses B and defers. What is this effect, and does basic RTS/CTS automatically authorise C to ignore the busy medium?

options.text: The hidden terminal problem; RTS/CTS fixes it
options.explanation: Hidden terminals are stations that *cannot* hear each other and collide. Here C *can* hear B and defers unnecessarily: the opposite problem.

options.text: Exposed-terminal deferral; basic RTS/CTS does not automatically authorise concurrent transmission
options.explanation: Correct. Deferral can suppress a potentially useful transmission, but basic protection is not a general spatial-reuse permission system.

options.text: The performance anomaly; airtime fairness fixes it
options.explanation: The performance anomaly is about slow clients consuming airtime, not about unnecessary deferral due to overheard transmissions.

options.text: Adjacent-channel interference; moving to channel 6 fixes it
options.explanation: All four stations are on the same channel here, and C defers because it decodes B. That is co-channel deferral, not adjacent-channel noise.

questions.workedExample: The question supplies non-interference at both data receivers; merely saying D cannot hear B would not establish that C cannot harm A. C still defers because it senses the medium. This is exposed-terminal deferral. ACK interference and protocol timing also matter, so basic RTS/CTS does not automatically prove a concurrent complete exchange is safe.

questions.prompt: A busy venue has compatible clients sending small packets plus older 2.4-GHz-only devices. Which measures directly multiplex clients within an access, allocate airtime more fairly, or move clients to separate contention resources, when supported and configured? Select all that apply.

options.text: Enabling OFDMA so the AP serves several clients' small frames in one transmission
options.explanation: Correct. Suitable OFDMA scheduling can multiplex compatible clients into one access; workload and scheduler behaviour determine the benefit.

options.text: Enabling airtime fairness on the APs
options.explanation: Correct as a potential mitigation. Airtime policies and traffic direction determine how much control the AP has; this does not guarantee elimination of every slow-client effect.

options.text: Steering capable clients onto 6 GHz, where legacy devices cannot operate
options.explanation: Correct where permitted and supported. This separates them from older 2.4/5-GHz-only clients, but 6 GHz is not interference-free or guaranteed to use high rates.

options.text: Enabling 1024-QAM
options.explanation: Higher QAM can shorten data airtime when signal quality permits, but does not directly combine clients’ separate channel accesses. Proximity alone is not the criterion.

options.text: Using 40 MHz channels on 2.4 GHz to double capacity
options.explanation: On 2.4 GHz a 40 MHz channel covers most of the band and overlaps neighbouring APs, causing interference across the hall.

questions.workedExample: OFDMA can amortise contention, airtime policies can improve scheduling, and another permitted band can separate clients into different contention resources. These are candidates for measurement, not a guaranteed ranking. Higher QAM addresses payload rate, while wider 2.4 GHz channels reduce the separate-channel choices available in a dense deployment.

questions.prompt: With numeric ping output to a home router, measured RTT rises from 4 ms idle to 180–250 ms during a download, without observed loss. Which leading hypothesis should be tested against local queue, retry and CPU measurements?

options.text: The download moves the router's radio to a longer-range channel with more propagation delay
options.explanation: Propagation delay over a few metres is nanoseconds. Channel choice does not add 200 ms.

options.text: The router is rate-limiting ICMP during heavy traffic
options.explanation: A token-bucket drop policy often causes loss, but ICMP scheduling or prioritisation can also affect latency. Do not exclude all router processing effects from the ping trace alone.

options.text: Load-induced queueing, potentially compounded by wireless retries or contention
options.explanation: Correct as a leading hypothesis, not a unique diagnosis. Locate the actual queue before choosing AQM, scheduling or shaping changes.

options.text: DNS lookups during the download slow ping down
options.explanation: With numeric output the measured RTT increase is not explained by reverse-name display lookups. Some ping modes do perform name lookups, so “ping never uses DNS” is too broad.

questions.workedExample: The load correlation suggests queueing or contention. As a hypothetical FIFO calculation, 2,000,000 queued bytes at 80 Mbit/s need 0.2 seconds to drain. The ping alone does not measure that backlog or prove all delay is bufferbloat. Compare wired tests, AP queue/retry counters and CPU load; choose mitigation for the actual bottleneck.

questions.prompt: In the lesson’s 5 GHz OFDM DCF example, why is SIFS (16 µs) shorter than DIFS (34 µs) for an acknowledged unicast exchange?

options.text: SIFS is shorter so that ACKs use less battery
options.explanation: Battery has nothing to do with it; the gap length is about priority on the channel.

options.text: It gives the immediate ACK priority over compliant DCF contenders that sense the exchange
options.explanation: Correct. The ACK can begin before their DIFS expires. Hidden terminals or interference can still disrupt it; this is priority, not an absolute collision-free guarantee.

options.text: SIFS allows the receiver time to decrypt the frame before acknowledging
options.explanation: SIFS includes turnaround/processing constraints, but the comparison with DIFS establishes access priority. It is not a guarantee that all security processing completes before ACK transmission.

options.text: DIFS is only used on 2.4 GHz; on 5 GHz everyone uses SIFS
options.explanation: The specified 5 GHz OFDM DCF model uses both gaps. Other PHYs and QoS access categories have their own timing parameters; contenders do not all use SIFS.

questions.workedExample: For the specified timings, DIFS = SIFS + 2 × slot = 16 + 2 × 9 = 34 µs. A receiver starting its ACK after 16 µs gains priority over compliant contenders that sense it and require 34 µs of idle time. This protects the exchange under those conditions; it is not an atomic guarantee against all other transmissions. Other PHYs and EDCA categories use different parameters.

lessons.title: 4G and 5G networks, and what they mean for apps
lessons.summary: How a phone's packets travel through the radio network and the mobile core, how the radio's power states affect latency and battery use, and how to write apps that behave well on cellular.
lessons.body:
Cellular systems centrally schedule much of their radio traffic, unlike basic Wi-Fi contention. This is a distinction in access mechanisms, not a guarantee of collision-free radio or predictable latency: random access, interference, coverage and load still matter. Cellular deployments can use licensed, shared or unlicensed spectrum; Wi-Fi also has scheduled multi-user modes.

For applications, mobile paths introduce changing capacity, radio-state transitions, possible address changes and provider-specific translation or filtering. Design for interruption and measure the devices and networks you support.

## The big picture

Every cellular network has three parts: the phone (the **UE**, user equipment), the **radio access network** (RAN) of base stations, and the **core network** that handles identity, sessions and the gateway to the Internet.

```
 UE ~~radio~~ eNodeB/gNodeB
                 |  (backhaul)
     +-----------+----------+
     | Core                 |
     |  control: MME / AMF  |
     |  sessions: SMF       |
     |  user plane:         |
     |  S-GW+P-GW / UPF ----+--> Internet
     +----------------------+
```

| Part | 4G (LTE / EPC) | 5G (NR / 5GC) |
|---|---|---|
| Base station | eNodeB | gNodeB |
| Attach, mobility | MME | AMF |
| Session control | distributed across MME and gateway control functions | SMF |
| Packet gateway | S-GW + P-GW | UPF |
| Subscriber data / authentication | HSS with associated authentication functions | UDM/UDR for subscriber data; AUSF for authentication |

The 5G core defines **service-based** control-plane functions with HTTP-based service interfaces. Not every interface is HTTP/2: user-plane tunnels and control interfaces such as N4 use other protocols. Functions can be virtualised; earlier generations also support virtualisation, so “5G software versus 4G fixed boxes” is misleading.

### Tunnels keep your IP address still

For an IP session, session establishment selects/allocates addressing and user-plane resources. LTE uses EPS bearers with a P-GW anchor. In 5G, the SMF manages the PDU session and address allocation, potentially using a UPF or external allocation mechanism; a session-anchor UPF forwards user traffic. Not every PDU session carries IP: Ethernet and unstructured types also exist. Relevant radio-to-core user-plane interfaces use **GTP-U**, whose registered destination UDP port is 2152.

The gateway is the **anchor**: to the Internet, your phone lives at the gateway. During a supported handover that preserves the session anchor/address, user-plane paths can be updated while the application retains its IP address. Connections can survive, but radio interruption, loss, session changes or timeout can still break them; no particular vehicle speed guarantees continuity.

Moving to an independently addressed Wi-Fi path commonly changes the effective endpoint address. Keeping the old path alive, provider-integrated access, tunnels or mobility-capable transports can change the outcome.

## Scheduled radio access

LTE and NR use OFDM-based downlink resource allocation. A resource block spans **12 subcarriers**; the number of active subcarriers depends on the channel configuration. In the conventional LTE example, 15 kHz spacing gives 180 kHz per resource block and a 1 ms subframe scheduling interval. Later features and specialised modes qualify a universal 1 ms rule. LTE uplink commonly uses DFT-spread OFDM (SC-FDMA), rather than simply the same downlink waveform.

For dynamically scheduled uplink data without an existing grant, a connected UE can request resources and receive an uplink grant. Existing/configured grants and random-access procedures mean a fresh request/grant is not required for every packet. Scheduling coordinates access but does not eliminate random-access collisions or inter-cell interference; fairness is a scheduler policy, not an automatic guarantee.

5G NR adds flexible **numerology**. Common examples use 15, 30, 60 or 120 kHz spacing. This is not the complete set in later releases. For normal cyclic prefix, the corresponding full-slot duration is `1 ms / 2^μ` with spacing `15 × 2^μ kHz`; mini-slot transmission need not occupy a full slot:

| Spacing | Slot length | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| 15 kHz | 1 ms | low band, wide coverage |
| 30 kHz | 0.5 ms | mid band (e.g. 3.5 GHz) |
| 120 kHz | 0.125 ms | mmWave |

### Spectrum: coverage versus capacity

NR specifications define release-specific frequency ranges, with different supported bandwidths and spacings:

- **FR1** includes low and mid bands. Lower frequencies often aid coverage, while wider available allocations can provide capacity; actual range depends on power, antennas and surroundings. A 3.5 GHz deployment is an illustrative mid-band case, not a universal regional allocation.
- **FR2** covers higher-frequency NR bands, commonly called mmWave in the industry, and has release-specific subdivisions. Wide channels and beamforming can support high capacity, but blockage and link budget matter. A fixed “few hundred metres” coverage rule is not reliable for every deployment.

> [!note] Why "5G" on your phone may be mostly 4G
> A common **NSA option 3** deployment uses LTE/EPC as the master/core with NR as secondary access. **SA option 2** connects NR to the 5G core. “NSA” has broader architectural usage, and a status icon alone does not prove which capabilities are active. Feature availability depends on release, configuration, device and operator support.

ITU IMT-2020 evaluation requirements include a 20 Gbit/s peak downlink data rate and 4 ms eMBB / 1 ms URLLC user-plane latency targets under their defined conditions. The latency measure is one-way radio user-plane latency, not an Internet ping RTT; the peak rate is not a per-user service guarantee. Scheduling, backhaul, core routing, server work and other path segments contribute to application latency.

## Radio power states and application traffic

Radio activity can contribute substantially to energy use, depending on the device and workload. **RRC** (Radio Resource Control) manages connection states:

```
            data to send
 RRC_IDLE ----------------> RRC_CONNECTED
 (no radio  promotion:      (scheduled,
  resources) signalling      fast, power
     ^       round trips      hungry)
     |                          |
     +--- inactivity timer -----+
          (the "tail")
```

- **Idle**: the UE has no active RRC connection, but can perform paging monitoring, measurements, reselection and other procedures. It is not powered off.
- **Connected**: RRC context supports scheduled communication; grants and discontinuous reception (DRX) still affect timing and power. Connected does not mean continuously transmitting or always at maximum power.
- NR **RRC_INACTIVE** retains access-stratum context and can reduce resumption work relative to idle. Its supported use is release/deployment-specific; related LTE suspension and newer inactive-state data features make “all packets always need full promotion” too broad.

Two costs follow:

1. **Promotion latency.** When ordinary user-plane transfer requires an idle UE to establish an RRC connection, random access, RRC setup and associated signalling add delay. A quiet period alone does not establish that this transition is required. The delay depends on radio state, procedures, release, coverage and load; no fixed millisecond value is guaranteed.
2. **Tail energy.** Activity can leave the radio in a higher-energy state after payload transfer ends. Timers, DRX and other state transitions determine the cost. Bursts can overlap or share radio activity; connected time is not identical to measured energy.

### Worked example: polling versus batching

Use a toy model: instantaneous requests each add an interval `[t, t + 10)` of activity. Count the union of those intervals. Ignore promotion time, transfers, DRX, other applications and observation-window clipping:

```python
from math import isfinite

def radio_on(times, tail=10.0):
    """Union length of tail intervals."""
    times = list(times)
    if not isfinite(tail) or tail < 0:
        raise ValueError("invalid tail")
    if any(not isfinite(t) for t in times):
        raise ValueError("invalid time")
    on, until = 0.0, None
    for t in sorted(times):
        if until is None or t > until:
            on += tail  # new promotion
        else:
            on += t + tail - until  # extend
        until = t + tail
    return on

hour = 3600
poll = list(range(0, hour, 30))
batch = list(range(0, hour, 300))
print(radio_on(poll), radio_on(batch))
# 1200.0 120.0
```

In this model, the supplied one-hour schedules produce 1,200 and 120 seconds of interval coverage. This is not a prediction of battery energy on a real phone. Nearby requests share intervals: `radio_on([0, 4, 8, 50])` returns 28 seconds, not 40.

> [!tip] Practical rules for mobile apps
> - Batch and prefetch: grouping delay-tolerant work can reduce repeated radio activity; avoid downloading unnecessary data.
> - Use the platform push service (APNs, FCM) instead of your own polling or keepalive. Platform-managed delivery can share infrastructure across apps; delivery timing and energy are not free or guaranteed.
> - Defer non-urgent uploads (analytics, logs) until the radio is already active or the device is on Wi-Fi and charging.
> - Expect the first request after idle to be slow; choose measured end-to-end deadlines and retry behaviour rather than assuming a constant first-request cost.

## Addresses, NAT and IPv6

**Carrier-grade NAT** (CGNAT) lets an operator share public IPv4 addresses among many subscribers. The number sharing one address and availability of public addressing vary. Possible consequences:

- Unsolicited inbound IPv4 connections are commonly restricted without suitable mappings/policies. Peer-to-peer applications can use ICE with STUN and, when needed, TURN relays; STUN itself is not a relay.
- NAT mappings expire after a period of idleness, according to protocol and operator policy. Long-lived idle TCP connections can silently die, which is one more reason to use the platform push service.
- Rate-limiting by public IP can group unrelated subscribers; combine appropriate account/token and abuse controls rather than treating an address as one person.

Operators can provide **IPv6-only** access with NAT64/DNS64 or **464XLAT** to reach IPv4 services. 464XLAT combines client-side stateless translation with network-side stateful translation. Apple’s IPv6-only compatibility guidance recommends hostnames and system APIs; some system APIs can synthesise an IPv6 destination even from an IPv4 literal. Raw IPv4-only socket code without translation/synthesis is a different case.

## Mobility between networks

If an application loses its cellular path and must use an independently addressed Wi-Fi path, ordinary TCP cannot simply change its endpoint tuple. Joining Wi-Fi alone does not necessarily close every existing cellular connection.

Ways to cope:

- **Retry idempotent requests** and make uploads resumable.
- **QUIC** identifies connections by a connection ID rather than the 4-tuple, so eligible client migration can preserve a confirmed connection when permitted and the new path works; validation and other conditions still apply.
- **Multipath TCP** can carry one connection over multiple subflows, for example Wi-Fi and cellular, when endpoints and policies support it. It improves mobility options without guaranteeing uninterrupted service.
- Use the OS's path monitoring (`NWPathMonitor` on iOS, `ConnectivityManager` on Android) to react to changes and to check whether the path is **expensive** or **constrained** under the platform’s definitions; these flags are not interchangeable with a simple cellular-versus-Wi-Fi test before downloading large media.

## Performance characteristics to design for

- **Bandwidth varies wildly**: with coverage, scheduling, congestion, device capabilities and backhaul. Use adaptive bitrate streaming and responsive images rather than assuming a speed.
- **Deep buffers**: large persistent queues on a mobile path can add substantial latency under load (bufferbloat); measure the location and size rather than assuming a particular base station buffer. BBR is model-based, using delivery-rate and RTT estimates; it is not simply delay-based and does not universally outperform CUBIC. CUBIC can also react to ECN rather than waiting only for loss.
- **Loss is mostly hidden**: HARQ and, where configured, acknowledged-mode RLC can recover some radio losses before TCP sees them. Retry limits and unacknowledged modes mean not every loss is hidden.
- **Handovers** can cause interruption or loss of varying duration. Design UIs that tolerate a request taking several seconds occasionally.

> [!warning] Testing only on office Wi-Fi
> An app that feels instant on a fast Wi-Fi network can be painful on a train. Use network link conditioners (Xcode's Network Link Conditioner, Android emulator network profiles) to test with high latency, low bandwidth and loss.

## Network slicing and edge computing

With standalone 5G, an operator can create **network slices**: logical networks with selected capabilities and policies; actual end-to-end guarantees require provisioned resources, isolation, admission control and an enforceable service agreement, for example one for low-latency industrial control and one for ordinary broadband, on the same infrastructure.

**Multi-access edge computing** (MEC) can place application compute nearer access networks, potentially reducing the path to a distant cloud region. Placement is not necessarily beside a UPF, and a nearby server alone does not guarantee low end-to-end latency.

## Key takeaways
- Cellular separates user equipment, radio access and core functions. Session anchoring can preserve addresses across supported handovers.
- Scheduled data access coexists with random access, configured grants and interference; cellular is not universally collision-free.
- NR numerology, architecture options and state behaviour are release- and configuration-dependent.
- Batching can reduce radio activity, but a fixed-tail model measures interval coverage, not battery energy.
- Plan for changing capacity, addressing, translation and interruptions. Migration-capable transports also have prerequisites.

> [!note] Evidence limits
> Fixed handover success speeds, radio-state timings, spectrum-wide range figures, operator market shares and guaranteed energy/latency improvements are omitted because no deployment evidence establishes them here. Complete release-specific band tables and advanced inactive-state data procedures are outside this lesson. No cellular modem or operator-network experiment was run.

questions.prompt: An RRC-connected LTE UE has uplink data, no usable existing or configured grant, and an available scheduling-request resource. In the ordinary dynamic scheduling path, what does it do before sending that data?

options.text: It listens for an idle channel, then waits a random backoff like Wi-Fi
options.explanation: The question describes cellular dynamic scheduling, not Wi-Fi contention. Cellular random access can itself involve contention, so “LTE has no contention anywhere” would be incorrect.

options.text: It sends a scheduling request, and the base station grants it specific uplink resource blocks
options.explanation: Correct. The eNodeB is a central scheduler. The phone asks, receives a grant for particular resource blocks and time slots, and only then transmits.

options.text: It transmits immediately; collisions are resolved by retransmission
options.explanation: Uncoordinated transmission would cause collisions between phones. LTE avoids that by scheduling uplink centrally.

options.text: It must first establish a new IP address with the core
options.explanation: Requesting uplink resources does not itself require allocating a new IP address; IP-session establishment is a separate procedure.

questions.workedExample: Under the supplied conditions the UE requests uplink scheduling and uses the granted resources. An existing grant, configured scheduling or random-access procedure can change the path, so a fresh request is not mandatory for every packet. Scheduling coordinates resources; it does not guarantee no interference or fixed request/grant latency.

questions.prompt: A user on a train hands over between six cells during a video call, but the call's IP address never changes. Which component makes that possible?

options.text: The base station (eNodeB/gNodeB), which assigns the IP address
options.explanation: A handover changes the serving radio resources and can occur between cells of the same base station. Session anchoring and path updates, rather than an assumed base-station address assignment, explain the retained address.

options.text: A preserved session anchor—P-GW in LTE or session-anchor UPF in 5G—with updated user-plane paths
options.explanation: Correct. Retaining the session’s addressing while updating radio-side paths can preserve connectivity; not every handover preserves every session.

options.text: DHCP leases that last longer than the journey
options.explanation: A long lease alone does not redirect the user-plane path during handover. Address-allocation methods can vary, including external mechanisms; anchoring and mobility procedures are the relevant distinction.

options.text: The phone's SIM card, which stores a fixed IP address
options.explanation: SIM credentials support subscriber identification and authentication. A fixed address stored on the SIM is not the session anchoring and path-update mechanism described here.

questions.workedExample: A session can retain its anchor and address while the network updates tunnels toward the serving radio node. LTE control functions or the 5G AMF/SMF coordinate the relevant procedures. A 5G UPF forwards user traffic while the SMF manages session/address-allocation procedures. Continuity is possible under the stated observation, not guaranteed for all handovers.

questions.prompt: A trace confirms that a phone starts an API request from RRC_IDLE and performs RRC setup before transmitting data. Subsequent requests use the connected state. Which cellular mechanism contributes to the first request’s extra delay?

options.text: The radio must be promoted from RRC idle to connected, which needs signalling round trips before data flows
options.explanation: Correct. Promotion from idle involves random access, RRC setup and security set-up. Subsequent requests find the radio already connected.

options.text: The base station has to download the app's data from the Internet first
options.explanation: Application fetching is not the radio-state transition established by the trace. Edge caching may exist in some deployments, but it does not explain the specified setup sequence.

options.text: The phone has to re-attach to the network and get a new IP address
options.explanation: RRC_IDLE does not by itself require loss of registration or session addressing. A full re-attach and new address are not implied by this transition.

options.text: LTE uses a slower modulation for the first packet
options.explanation: Link adaptation can depend on channel estimates and scheduler policy. The supplied trace specifically establishes RRC setup; it does not establish a special first-packet modulation rule.

questions.workedExample: The trace establishes a radio-state transition: random access and RRC setup occur before the request’s data transmission. Later traffic can avoid that setup while the required context remains usable. Actual delay depends on configuration and conditions; a slow first request without such a trace could also involve DNS, transport/TLS setup or server work.

questions.prompt: Using the lesson's model (radio stays connected for a 10 s tail after each request; requests extending an existing tail only add the extra time), how many seconds is the radio connected for requests at t = 0, 3, 20, 25 and 60 s?

options.explanation: That counts a full 10 s tail for each of the five requests, ignoring that requests at 3 s and 25 s fall inside an existing tail.
Correct. 10 (t=0) + 3 (t=3 extends to 13) + 10 (t=20) + 5 (t=25 extends 30 to 35) + 10 (t=60) = 38 s.
The three interval unions have lengths 13, 15 and 10 seconds, totalling 38; 33 undercounts their combined duration.
That is the span from first to last request, as if the radio stayed on throughout. It returns to idle between 35 s and 60 s.

questions.workedExample:
Walk through the timeline, tracking when the tail ends:

```
t=0   new: +10  on=10  until=10
t=3   3<=10: +3 on=13  until=13
t=20  20>13: +10 on=23 until=30
t=25  25<=30: +5 on=28 until=35
t=60  60>35: +10 on=38 until=70
```

Total: **38 s**. Grouping requests means they share tails: the two clusters cost 13 s and 15 s, while the isolated request at 60 s costs a full 10 s.

questions.prompt: Use the lesson’s isolated 10-second-tail model. A background app sends a 200-byte heartbeat every 20 seconds, but its requirements permit minutes of delay and platform push for incoming notifications. Which redesign best reduces the model’s repeated activity intervals?

options.text: Compress the heartbeat to 50 bytes
options.explanation: The supplied fixed-tail model assigns the same interval to each request regardless of payload. Real energy consumption also depends on transfer size and radio behaviour.

options.text: Switch the heartbeat from TCP to UDP
options.explanation: Changing the transport alone does not remove the model’s one interval per heartbeat. Real transport behaviour can affect traffic and energy.

options.text: Drop the heartbeat, batch uploads every few minutes, and use the platform push service for server-to-device messages
options.explanation: Correct for the stated delay-tolerant requirements. Less frequent batching reduces isolated fixed-tail intervals; platform push can avoid a separate polling scheme but is not energy-free.

options.text: Send the heartbeat more often so the radio never goes idle, avoiding promotion costs
options.explanation: More frequent activity merges intervals into more continuous coverage in this model. Real devices have DRX and power states not represented here.

questions.workedExample: A 20-second period with isolated 10-second tails covers 50% of time in the toy model; a 300-second period covers about 3.3%. This is not a measured battery reduction. Platform-managed push may share infrastructure across apps, but still has delivery, activity and energy costs.

questions.prompt: A download uses ordinary TCP without MPTCP or an address-preserving tunnel. It survives cell handovers with the same anchored address. The old cellular path is then lost and traffic must use a new Wi-Fi endpoint address; the connection fails. Which explanation fits?

options.text: Wi-Fi uses a different MTU, which TCP cannot adjust to
options.explanation: PMTU problems can cause failures, but the stated endpoint-address change directly prevents ordinary TCP from simply continuing with the original tuple.

options.text: Joining Wi-Fi gives the phone a new IP address from a different network, so the TCP 4-tuple no longer matches
options.explanation: Correct under the supplied conditions. Joining Wi-Fi alone does not necessarily destroy every cellular connection if its original path remains usable.

options.text: Home routers block downloads that started on another network
options.explanation: A new router may have stateful policies, but no general rule identifies where an application download began. The given tuple change is the relevant mechanism.

options.text: The cellular network sends a TCP reset when the phone leaves
options.explanation: A reset is not required for this failure; losing the usable old path can leave the connection unable to progress.

questions.workedExample: Supported cell handovers preserved the session address. The later forced change to an independently addressed path cannot retarget an ordinary TCP connection. The application can reconnect and resume if its protocol supports that. QUIC migration or MPTCP may preserve transport continuity when their prerequisites are satisfied.

questions.prompt: Your API rate-limits to 100 requests per minute per client IP. Mobile users on one operator start receiving HTTP 429s, even light users. Which statements about carrier networks are relevant or true? Select all that apply.

options.text: With carrier-grade NAT, thousands of phones can share one public IPv4 address, so they share your per-IP limit
options.explanation: Correct. Shared addressing can combine unrelated users under one limit. Account/token controls can help, alongside appropriate unauthenticated-abuse controls.

options.text: Phones behind CGNAT generally cannot accept unsolicited inbound connections
options.explanation: Correct as a general tendency, subject to mappings and filtering policy. ICE can use STUN for discovery/checks and TURN for relaying; STUN is not itself a relay.

options.text: CGNAT mappings for idle flows can expire, silently breaking long-lived idle TCP connections
options.explanation: Correct. Expiration can disrupt an idle connection. Later traffic may be dropped, rejected or create another mapping, depending on the NAT and packet; continued TCP connectivity is not assured.

options.text: IPv6-only mobile networks cannot reach IPv4-only servers at all
options.explanation: Translation can provide connectivity. Hostnames and suitable APIs are useful, while 464XLAT or address-synthesis APIs can also support some IPv4-literal applications.

options.text: CGNAT gives each packet from a phone a different public address
options.explanation: Mappings are kept per flow (and often per subscriber) for the life of the mapping; changing per packet would break every TCP connection.

questions.workedExample: CGNAT can make unrelated users share a public address and therefore a per-IP limit. Mappings/filtering can restrict inbound traffic and idle mappings can expire. An IPv6-only access network can still reach IPv4 services through translation. These are possibilities to investigate, not proof that every observed 429 has this cause.

questions.prompt: For an NR normal-cyclic-prefix full slot, use spacing 15 × 2^μ kHz and duration 1 ms / 2^μ. What duration corresponds to 60 kHz, and what can wider spacing enable?

options.text: 0.5 ms; wider spacing gives better coverage
options.explanation: 0.5 ms is the slot at 30 kHz (μ = 1). And wider spacing shortens symbols, which suits high bands and low latency, not long-range coverage.

options.text: 0.25 ms; shorter symbol/slot durations can support faster scheduling and mitigate some high-frequency impairments
options.explanation: Correct. μ = 2, so the full slot is 0.25 ms. Actual latency, supported numerologies and trade-offs depend on configuration and band.

options.text: 4 ms; wider spacing means longer slots
options.explanation: The relationship is inverse: doubling spacing halves the slot length.

options.text: 1 ms; slot length is fixed in 5G as in LTE
options.explanation: The supplied NR formula gives different slot durations. Conventional LTE uses 1 ms subframes, but later shortened-TTI features also make a universal LTE timing claim too broad.

questions.workedExample: 60 / 15 = 4 = 2², so μ = 2 and the normal-CP full slot lasts 1/4 ms. The table gives 1, 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 ms for μ = 0–3. Wider spacing can support shorter transmission scheduling and different impairment trade-offs; it does not guarantee a particular application RTT. Later NR releases include additional spacings and mini-slot operation.

questions.prompt: In a laboratory, an IPv6-only host has NAT64/DNS64 but no CLAT. Raw AF_INET socket code tries to connect to a lab IPv4-only server; it does not call an address-synthesis API. A hostname-based AF_UNSPEC client reaches that same server through a DNS64-synthesised AAAA record. Why does the raw IPv4 attempt fail?

options.text: The server does not support IPv6
options.explanation: The successful translated connection demonstrates that this IPv4-only server is reachable through NAT64. The raw IPv4 socket path lacks the required translation/synthesis.

options.text: The raw IPv4 socket has no usable IPv4 path, while the other client obtains an IPv6 destination that the NAT64 gateway can translate
options.explanation: Correct for the explicitly specified API path. Some Apple/system APIs can synthesise addresses even for literals, so a literal alone would not prove failure.

options.text: Plain HTTP is blocked on IPv6-only networks
options.explanation: HTTP versus HTTPS has nothing to do with IP versions here; the failure is reaching the address at all.

options.text: NAT64 only translates traffic on port 443
options.explanation: NAT64 is not restricted to port 443. Reachability still depends on supported protocols, mappings and policy; here the raw socket lacks a usable translated path.

questions.workedExample: DNS64 can synthesise an AAAA answer for an IPv4-only name, giving the IPv6 client a destination routed to NAT64. The specified raw IPv4 code neither obtains that address nor has client-side translation. Prefer suitable system APIs and hostnames; do not infer failure merely from the presence of an IPv4 literal in a high-level URL. HTTP security policy is separate from this IP-layer experiment.

questions.prompt: You are designing a voice-call app that must keep a call running when the user walks out of Wi-Fi coverage onto 5G. Which approaches genuinely help? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use QUIC, whose connection IDs let a connection migrate to a new client address
options.explanation: Correct as a capability: eligible QUIC client migration requires permitted migration, suitable connection IDs, a working path and validation. It is not a zero-interruption guarantee.

options.text: Use Multipath TCP so subflows on Wi-Fi and cellular can carry the same connection
options.explanation: Correct when endpoints, operating systems and application policies support MPTCP subflows on those paths.

options.text: Rely on the cellular core's GTP tunnels to keep the Wi-Fi IP address
options.explanation: Ordinary independent Wi-Fi is not automatically anchored by the cellular core. Integrated non-3GPP access or mobility services can exist, so this must not be assumed without deployment support.

options.text: Enable TCP keepalives every 5 seconds
options.explanation: Keepalives can help detect some failures, but cannot migrate ordinary TCP across an endpoint-address change. Frequent probes add traffic and may increase energy use.

options.text: Monitor path changes with the OS API and re-establish the media session quickly when the path changes
options.explanation: Correct as an approach to detect change and trigger recovery. Callback timing and reconnection are not guaranteed to complete in a fraction of a second.

questions.workedExample: Migration-capable transports and application-level reconnection/resumption can improve mobility. Each depends on supported paths and endpoint behaviour. Keepalives can help detect some failures but cannot change ordinary TCP endpoint addresses. An independent Wi-Fi path does not automatically inherit a cellular session anchor.

questions.prompt: An upload coincides with RTT increasing from 45 to 700 ms on a cellular path, with little observed packet loss. Which is a plausible hypothesis and measurement-led response, rather than a conclusion proved by ping alone?

options.text: The upload makes the phone switch to a farther cell; nothing can be done
options.explanation: The observation does not establish a handover. A few additional kilometres of propagation alone cannot explain hundreds of milliseconds; scheduling, retransmissions, queues and other path effects need investigation.

options.text: A standing queue may be delaying packets; locate it and test pacing, queue management or traffic limits under representative load
options.explanation: Correct. Radio retries, scheduling and processing may also contribute. BBR is model-based, and switching algorithms is not a guaranteed cure.

options.text: The core network deprioritises ICMP during uploads
options.explanation: ICMP handling could affect the observation and should be checked. A steady load-correlated increase alone does not exclude it.

options.text: TCP's slow start adds 650 ms of delay per round trip
options.explanation: Slow start affects how fast the sender ramps up; it does not add a fixed delay to other packets.

questions.workedExample: If the extra 0.65 seconds were entirely a FIFO backlog at a constant 8 Mbit/s, it would correspond to 8e6 × 0.65 / 8 = 650,000 bytes. That is a conditional estimate, not a measured queue size. CUBIC can respond to ECN as well as loss; BBR can also build queues. TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT limits unsent local buffering notifications/acceptance behaviour, not all in-flight traffic or a remote queue.

questions.prompt: An operator uses NSA option 3 with an LTE master and EPC. A customer requests the 5GC-defined slice-selection and session framework. What architectural component is missing from that deployment?

options.text: NSA cannot use mid-band spectrum
options.explanation: Option 3 can use supported NR bands such as mid band; it is not inherently restricted to one frequency range.

options.text: The 5G core and its slice-aware functions; option 3 still uses EPC
options.explanation: Correct. Moving to a suitable 5GC deployment enables the relevant framework, but does not itself guarantee end-to-end latency or isolation.

options.text: NSA phones cannot reach the Internet without Wi-Fi
options.explanation: NSA phones have full Internet access; the control plane simply runs over LTE.

options.text: Slicing requires mmWave
options.explanation: Slicing is a core and orchestration feature independent of frequency band.

questions.workedExample: NSA option 3 combines an LTE master/EPC with NR secondary radio access. SA option 2 connects NR to 5GC, which provides the requested framework. Other deployment options and EPC service differentiation exist. A factory latency guarantee additionally requires provisioned radio/transport/core resources, supported devices, application design and an appropriate service agreement.

lessons.title: Data-centre networks: leaf-spine, ECMP and oversubscription
lessons.summary: Why many data centres use Clos fabrics, how ECMP spreads flows across equal paths, and how to calculate oversubscription, scale and the cost of a failed spine.
lessons.body:
A service request may fan out to authentication, caches, databases and other services. This can create substantial **east–west** traffic between servers, alongside **north–south** traffic entering or leaving the facility. The actual traffic mix is workload-dependent.

Classic enterprise networks were built for north–south traffic: a hierarchy that funnels traffic between aggregation branches through a core. A common alternative is a **leaf-spine** fabric, a folded **Clos** topology. Under the simple fully connected model below, each leaf pair has multiple paths of equal configured routing cost, not necessarily identical delay or available bandwidth.

## Why the tree broke

The traditional design had three layers:

```
         [core]     [core]
        /      \   /      \
     [agg]    [agg]     [agg]
     / \       / \       / \
  [acc][acc][acc][acc][acc][acc]
   |    |    |    |    |    |
  servers in racks
```

Problems for east–west traffic:

- **Bottlenecks up the tree.** Traffic between racks in different branches must climb to the core, so aggregate demand can exceed upstream capacity. The required equipment depends on the scale and traffic design.
- **Spanning Tree.** Layer 2 designs ran the Spanning Tree Protocol to prevent loops, which works by *blocking* redundant links. A redundant pair may have only one forwarding path for a particular spanning-tree instance; not every design strands exactly half of all capacity.
- **Uneven latency.** Two servers might be one hop apart or five, depending on where they sit.

## Leaf-spine: a folded Clos network

In 1953 Charles Clos showed how to build large non-blocking telephone switches out of many small ones arranged in stages. Data centres apply the same idea to packet switches:

```
  [S1]   [S2]   [S3]   [S4]   spines
   |\ \  /| |\  /| |\  / /|
   (every leaf to every spine)
   |/ /  \| |/  \| |/  \ \|
  [L1]   [L2]   [L3]   [L4]   leaves
   ||     ||     ||     ||
 servers servers servers servers
```

- In this example each rack has one **leaf** switch; real designs may use dual attachment or other placements.
- Every leaf connects to **every** spine. Spines do not connect to each other, and leaves do not connect to leaves.
- A path between these different leaves traverses three switches: source leaf → spine → destination leaf. Service chains, other fabric tiers and same-leaf traffic differ.
- Between two leaves there are as many equal paths as there are spines. With 4 spines, 4 paths.

Such fabrics can use fixed-port switches, which need not be identical. Adding spines also needs ports and links on every participating leaf. Adding leaves consumes spine ports; cost and topology limits remain.

Links are normally **layer 3** (routed), not layer 2. Each switch runs a routing protocol; RFC 7938 describes the common choice of eBGP, with an ASN allocation scheme suited to the topology and loop-prevention policy. L3 ECMP can use redundant links without STP blocking, but convergence, route limits and failure containment require appropriate design. Where tenants need layer 2 segments, an overlay such as VXLAN carries them over the routed fabric (covered in the SDN lesson).

## ECMP: using all the paths

With routing, a leaf sees, say, four routes to the destination rack's prefix, all with the same cost. **Equal-cost multi-path** (ECMP) can install multiple eligible next hops, subject to configuration and implementation limits. The forwarding lookup selects a next hop for each packet, commonly using a flow-stable hash.

Choosing per *packet* can reorder TCP segments, which TCP treats as possible loss. A common policy therefore selects per **flow**: they hash header fields, usually the 5-tuple, and use the hash to pick a next hop.

```python
import zlib

def pick_uplink(flow, n_paths):
    if (type(n_paths) is not int
            or n_paths < 1):
        raise ValueError("bad path count")
    key = "|".join(map(str, flow)).encode()
    return zlib.crc32(key) % n_paths

flows = [("10.0.1.5", 40001 + i,
          "10.0.9.7", 443, "tcp")
         for i in range(6)]
print([pick_uplink(f, 4) for f in flows])
# [1, 3, 2, 2, 3, 1]
```

With unchanged inputs and next-hop mapping, a flow selects the same next hop. This avoids reordering caused by this path selector but does not guarantee no reordering elsewhere or during changes. Distinct flows can have different keys and still collide. Note that uplink 0 got nothing here: hashing is statistical, not a perfect balance.

### Where ECMP goes wrong

**Elephant flows collide.** With well-distributed keys and enough similarly sized flows, hashing can spread load approximately evenly. A few large flows (backups, replication, ML training) can land on the same link while others sit idle.

> [!example] How lumpy is hashing?
> Assume 8 equal flows choose independently and uniformly among 8 paths. The chance that every path gets exactly one is 8!/8⁸ ≈ 0.24%. The expected number of paths with no flow is 8 × (7/8)⁸ ≈ 2.7, so about a third of paths are empty on average in this model. Actual unused bandwidth also depends on flow demand and other traffic.

Mitigations include **flowlet switching** (changing path after a gap intended to exceed the path-delay difference; the guarantee depends on that delay bound), congestion-aware load balancing in the fabric, and **packet spraying** with transports that tolerate reordering. Applications can also split big transfers over several connections.

**Rehashing on failure.** If a switch picks `hash mod N` and one of four paths fails, it switches to `hash mod 3`. For uniform hashes and a stable ordering of the three surviving next hops, about a quarter of all flows keep their old physical path: most flows on *healthy* links move too, potentially causing reordering or disrupting unsynchronised per-flow state, such as a fleet of stateful load balancers behind ECMP. **Resilient hashing** aims to minimise remapping and can preserve healthy assignments on a simple removal. Bucket policies, rebalancing and implementation details determine whether additional flows move.

**Polarisation.** Correlated hash choices across tiers can underuse some paths, especially with matching path counts and mappings. Different hash seeds or inputs can reduce this polarisation.

## Oversubscription maths

A leaf has downlinks to servers and uplinks to spines. The **oversubscription ratio** compares them:

```
oversub = server-facing bandwidth
          / spine-facing bandwidth
```

### Worked example

A leaf has 48 × 25 Gbit/s server ports and 6 × 100 Gbit/s uplinks, one to each of 6 spines. Each spine has 64 × 100 Gbit/s ports.

```
down:  48 x 25  = 1200 Gbit/s
up:     6 x 100 =  600 Gbit/s
oversub = 1200 / 600 = 2:1

leaves  = spine ports      = 64
servers = 64 x 48          = 3072
uplinks = 64 leaves x 600 = 38.4 Tbit/s
```

The last line sums one-direction leaf uplink capacities; it is not a statement of bisection bandwidth or guaranteed delivered traffic. **2:1** means offered off-rack line-rate demand can be twice the aggregate uplink capacity. With equal sharing and no other bottleneck, 600/48 = 12.5 Gbit/s per server; ECMP does not guarantee that allocation. Direct same-leaf traffic avoids these uplinks, but service chaining or dual-attachment policy can differ.

A 1:1 leaf port ratio provides more uplink headroom than 2:1 or 4:1, but is not by itself proof that every traffic matrix runs without blocking. Routing, hash collisions, destination limits and other stages matter. Choose ratios using measured demand, failure headroom and cost; no universal workload-to-ratio rule is assumed here.

### Failure maths

Lose one of the six spines:

```
up:   5 x 100 = 500 Gbit/s
oversub = 1200 / 500 = 2.4:1
capacity lost = 1/6 = ~17%
```

With only this one spine failure and all remaining links/leaves working, racks retain topological connectivity after routing converges. Convergence time and transient packet loss are not guaranteed by the topology alone. Compare a design with 2 big spines, where one failure halves capacity. **More, smaller spines** give smaller blast radii, which is one of the strongest arguments for wide Clos fabrics.

### Scaling past one spine layer

The number of leaves is capped by spine port count. To go further, data centres add a third tier: groups of leaves and spines form **pods**, and a **super-spine** layer connects the pods. This is a 5-stage Clos.

For even k, the classic academic version is the **k-ary fat-tree** (Al-Fares et al., 2008), built entirely from k-port switches:

```
pods            = k
hosts           = k^3 / 4
k = 48: 48^3/4  = 27,648 hosts
```

Real examples include Facebook's 2014 data-centre fabric (server pods of 48 racks with four fabric switches each, connected by four planes of spine switches) and Google's Jupiter, which the 2015 *Jupiter Rising* paper described as delivering more than 1 Pbit/s of bisection bandwidth.

## Inside-the-fabric problems

- **Incast.** Concurrent replies can create a short burst exceeding a destination port’s service rate and available buffer. Loss may then trigger fast recovery, RACK/TLP or an RTO, depending on the trace and stack. Linux’s documented global default minimum RTO is 200 ms, but route/socket settings and newer configurable controls can alter it; not every tail loss waits for that timeout.
- **Finite buffers.** Switch buffer capacity and allocation vary by model. Burst demand and shared-buffer contention matter even when average utilisation is low.
- **Fixes.** **DCTCP** estimates the fraction of marked bytes and adjusts its congestion window proportionally, aiming to keep queues short; some RoCE deployments combine priority flow control with congestion notification; RDMA does not universally require PFC, and PFC introduces head-of-line/deadlock risks that require engineering. Applications can stagger fan-out replies or limit outstanding requests.

> [!tip] Reading a utilisation graph
> A link showing 30% average utilisation over five minutes can still drop packets: microbursts lasting a millisecond overflow a shallow buffer and vanish in the average. Look at drop counters and queue depth, not just utilisation.

## Trade-offs at a glance

| Choice | Benefit | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| More spines | capacity, small failure blast | ports, optics |
| Lower oversub | headroom for bursts | money |
| L3 + ECMP | no blocked links | L2 needs overlay |
| Per-flow hash | avoids selector-induced reordering while mapping is stable | elephant collisions |

## Key takeaways
- A fully connected two-tier leaf-spine model offers one path through each spine between different leaves.
- Routed ECMP can use parallel paths, but hashing does not guarantee equal utilisation or congestion-free service.
- Flowlets and resilient hashing reduce particular remapping/reordering problems under their assumptions.
- Oversubscription compares aggregate port capacities. Actual delivered rates, bisection capacity and failure recovery require separate analysis.
- Larger Clos fabrics add tiers. Incast and bursts need queue measurements, transport analysis and appropriate traffic controls.

> [!note] Evidence limits
> Universal data-centre traffic percentages, switch-buffer sizes, workload oversubscription ratios and fixed recovery times are omitted because no applicable deployment measurements were established. The capacity, hash and probability examples are models, not hardware benchmarks. This review did not measure fabric convergence, switch queues or an RDMA deployment.
